newsitem.title: UK: West pressures Milosevic but sanctions unlikely.
newsitem.headline: West pressures Milosevic but sanctions unlikely.

text.p: The West is keeping up the pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic following the violent police crackdown on protesters, but fresh sanctions to force him into submission are unlikely at this stage.

Diplomats say Russian opposition to such a move, combined with fears that more sanctions would simply hurt ordinary people, mean the West has only limited options. Opposition leaders had asked Western countries to refrain from sanctions, they said.

Instead, the United States and European allies are continuing to insist that Milosevic recognise opposition gains in last year's disputed municipal elections, while warning him that the future prosperity of Serbia is at stake and boosting support for the opposition Zajedno coalition.
"Our options are limited, despite the latest violent turn it has taken," one Western diplomat said.

With unrest rampant throughout the Balkans, European nations are increasingly worried that the violence in Belgrade could spiral out of control or that renewed tensions in the Kosovo region could touch off wider trouble beyond Serbia's borders.

Those fears were underlined on Monday, just hours after Milosevic's security police injured more than 100 protesters. Vuk Draskovic, one of the main opposition leaders, urged people to arm themselves for another demonstration.

Despite the growing risk of chaos after nearly three months of protests, diplomats say there is little the outside world can do, especially since Milosevic appears determined to make no further concessions and does not yet appear to be defeated.

Officials from the "contact group" of major powers -- the United States, Russia, France, Germany and Britain -- met over the weekend in the Swiss resort of Davos and agreed to maintain the political pressure on Milosevic, diplomats said.
Not even expelling the Yugoslav state -- Serbia and tiny Montenegro -- from international organisations is an option.
Although sanctions imposed on Belgrade in 1992 because of the war were lifted following the Bosnian peace agreement, Yugoslavia remains barred or suspended from most international bodies.
"At least we can withhold many of the good things that would come from such links for as long as this continues," said another Western envoy, who asked not to be identified.
Germany, France and Britain all denounced the violence in Belgrade on Monday.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel warned Milosevic that his country could not expect closer ties with Europe, while France said it would officially recognise the opposition leaders and invite them for talks in Paris.
The problem for Western nations is that they will face growing pressure to do more against Milosevic if the violence gets worse.

At that point, diplomats say there could be a major row with Russia, which has traditionally supported the Serbian leadership. Moscow says that the problems in Serbia are internal questions and generally refrains from joining in the chorus of criticism from the West.

The last thing the West wants is another row with Moscow over how to handle the Balkans, since NATO is desperately trying to reassure Moscow that the alliance's plans to expand into Eastern Europe do not represent a threat.
